title: Caching and cache stampedes
subtitle: A cache makes reads fast and cheap, until one popular key expires and every request rushes to the database at once.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is common. A shopping app runs a
flash sale
at 8 pm. The product page for one phone gets 5,000 requests a second.
The page data sits in Redis with a
TTL
of 60 seconds. The database is sized for the normal load: a few hundred queries a second. This works while the
cache
answers almost every read.
At 8:01 pm the key expires. In the next 200 ms, about a thousand requests find nothing in the cache. Each one runs the same heavy query against the database.
The database slows down, so the queries take longer. More requests miss while they wait, and they also go to the database. The product page times out, and the sale page shows errors for ten minutes.
Nothing was wrong with the code or the cache. One popular key expired at the worst moment.
A cache is a fast copy of data that is slow or costly to get. You read the copy instead of asking the database every time. A
cache hit
is fast. A cache miss means you must go to the source.
Every cache has to answer three questions:
How does data get in?
The app fills it, or the cache fills itself.
When does data leave?
It expires (TTL), it is deleted on a write (
invalidation
), or it is pushed out when memory is full (
eviction
What happens on a miss?
If a key is popular, a miss is not one query. It can be thousands.
The key idea.
A cache does not just make reads faster. It hides load. When a hot key expires, all that hidden load hits the database at once. Design for that moment.
That moment is called a
cache stampede
. A popular item expires, and many requests miss and rebuild the same item at the same time.
The Facebook memcache paper calls a similar problem a thundering herd: writes keep deleting a
hot key
, so many reads go to the database.
Ways to fill a cache
Cache-aside
The app checks the cache. On a miss, the app reads the database and writes the value into the cache. Facebook uses its memcache this way. On a write, it updates the database and then deletes the
cache key
. It deletes instead of updating because deletes are
idempotent
Read-through
The app only talks to the cache. On a miss, the cache itself loads from the database.
Write-through
Each write goes to the cache and the database together. The cache stays fresh, but every write is slower.
Write-behind
Writes go to the cache first and reach the database later, in batches. Writes are fast, but you can lose data if the cache dies first.

AWS calls a cache that the app code manages a "side cache", like cache-aside. Read-through and write-through are "inline caches". With an inline cache, the app needs no cache code. But if the cache fails, the app cannot work around it.
TTL, invalidation and eviction
A TTL sets how long a value lives. Pick it from two facts: how old the data may be, and how often the source changes. Then measure cache hits and misses, and adjust.
Invalidation removes a key when the data changes. It keeps data fresh, but you must find every place that writes the data.
Eviction removes keys when memory is full. In Redis you set a
maxmemory
limit and a policy.
allkeys-lru
removes the least recently used keys. Redis calls it a good default when some keys are read far more often than others.
The stampede, step by step
Step through what happens when a hot key expires. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Now try it yourself. Turn
request coalescing
on and off, and change the traffic.
Four ways to stop a stampede
1. Request coalescing (single-flight).
Only one load runs per key. Others wait for it and share the answer. Go's
singleflight
package does exactly this inside one server.
AWS uses coalescing so only one request is pending for an uncached item.
2. Locks or
leases
in the cache.

Coalescing inside one server still leaves one query per server. With 200 servers, that is 200 queries. A shared lock in the cache fixes this. Facebook's memcache gives out a "lease" token on a miss. By default, it gives at most one token per key every 10 seconds. Other clients are told to wait a moment and try again.
In Facebook's case, the herd came from writes that kept deleting a hot key. Over one week, for keys prone to thundering herds, peak database load fell from 17,000 to 1,300 queries a second.
3. Refresh early, with randomness.

Refresh a hot key a little before it expires, so it never goes missing. If every server refreshes at the same moment, you get a smaller stampede. So each request decides at random, and the chance rises as expiry gets closer.
Also add
jitter
to TTLs, so keys loaded together do not all expire together.
4. Serve stale while you refresh.

Keep the old value a little longer and return it while a refresh runs in the background. Serving stale data does not by itself limit the refresh to one request. Add coalescing or a lock, so only one request fetches the new value. HTTP has a header for serving stale data:
stale-while-revalidate
. With
max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30
, a response is fresh for 600 seconds. A cache may then serve it stale for 30 more seconds while it checks for a new copy.
AWS describes a similar idea: refresh after a "soft" TTL, and keep using the old value until a "hard" TTL if the source fails.
Request coalescing in each server
Partly. One query per server, not one in total.
Small code change.
Always, as a first step.
Lock or lease in the shared cache
One query in total.
Waiting clients add latency. Lost locks need a timeout.
Many servers and very hot keys.
Early refresh with jitter
, for keys that are read often.
Some extra loads before they are needed.
Hot keys you can predict.
Stale-while-revalidate
, with coalescing. Users get the old value fast.
Users may see data a few seconds old.
Data where a little staleness is fine, like product pages.
Longer TTL only
It only makes stampedes rarer.
More stale data.
Data that rarely changes.
Simple rule:
add coalescing everywhere. For your top keys, add
stale-while-revalidate
or a lease too.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask in design reviews:
"What happens to the database if the cache is empty?"
If the answer is "it crashes", you depend on the cache. Plan for a cold start.
Know your hot keys. Track the top keys by reads. A sale, a viral post or a homepage banner creates new ones.
Decide how stale each kind of data may be. Write it down: "prices: 5 seconds, product text: 10 minutes".
Watch hit rate, evictions and database load on the same dashboard. A falling hit rate is an early warning.
Never flush the whole cache in production without a plan. It turns every key into a miss at once.
Cache "not found" and error results too, with a short TTL. Otherwise a missing item sends every request to the database. AWS suggests a separate TTL for error results.
"Wrap this getProduct function with cache-aside in Redis. Use request coalescing so only one database call runs per key at a time."
"Add a soft TTL and a hard TTL. After the soft TTL, return the cached value and refresh it in the background. Add 10% random jitter to both."
"Write a load test where 1,000 requests ask for the same key just after it expires. Assert that the database gets at most 1 query."
The coalescing key is the cache key, not something that differs per user.
A failed or slow load does not leave other callers waiting forever. There is a
timeout
A lock in Redis has an expiry, so a crashed server does not hold it forever.
On a write, the code deletes or updates the cache
after
the database commit.
Error results are not cached for as long as good results.

q.v: In cache-aside, what does the app do on a cache miss?

options.v: Returns an error to the user.
Reads from the database, then puts the value in the cache.
Waits until the cache fills itself.

why.v: In cache-aside, the app owns the cache. It reads the database on a miss and fills the cache itself.

q.v: A key read 5,000 times a second expires. Each database query takes 200 ms. Without protection, what happens?

options.v: One request reloads it, the rest wait.
Many requests miss at the same moment and all run the same query.
The cache returns the old value automatically.

why.v: That is a cache stampede. Every request that misses before the first reload finishes goes to the database.

options.v: Sends one database query per key and lets other callers wait for its answer.
Joins many keys into one big key.
Spreads TTLs out with random values.

why.v: Only one load runs per key. Duplicate callers wait and get the same result.

options.v: So keys written at the same time do not all expire at the same time.
To make the cache use less memory.
So the cache never serves old data.

why.v: Keys loaded together, for example after a deploy, would expire together and cause a burst of misses.
